vignette: Sai, a 34-year-old South Eastern Asian chaplain, has been struggling with intense anxiety and intrusive memories following a traumatic mugging in his local community center. The event left him feeling deeply shaken and changed the way he perceives both himself and the world around him. On that fateful day, Sai was walking through a crowded section of the community center when he heard heavy breathing behind him. Suddenly, a masked individual appeared from the shadows and demanded his wallet and watch. Despite fighting back with all his strength, the mugger overpowered him, leaving Sai feeling helpless and violated. The incident left an indelible mark on his psyche, particularly because it happened in a place he had always considered safe. Since then, crowded places have become unbearable for Sai. Whenever he finds himself surrounded by people, he is immediately transported back to that moment in the community center. He remembers the heavy breathing as if it were happening again now, and the images of the mugger's face and the feeling of helplessness flood his mind. This recurring memory has left him with intense rage, often wondering why he wasn't able to fight off the attacker more effectively. Sai's self-blame is palpable; he feels that the event happened because of who he is-a vulnerable person unable to protect himself. He believes that someone else would not have gotten into this situation, and this belief exacerbates his feelings of helplessness and vulnerability. This sense of being helpless has extended beyond just the traumatic event itself, leading him to avoid situations where he might feel similarly overwhelmed or powerless. His negative appraisals are also reinforced by the vivid memories that continue to surface when he encounters triggers such as crowded places and heavy breathing sounds. These triggers not only bring back the visual images from that day but also intensify his sense of helplessness and character blame, creating a self-reinforcing cycle. When Sai remembers the event, he is overwhelmed with rage and a renewed belief that he cannot prevent bad things from happening to him. Sai's work as a chaplain has been significantly affected by these symptoms. He used to thrive in community settings, leading group prayers and offering comfort to those in need. However, since the mugging, he finds it almost impossible to be around large groups of people without feeling an intense sense of dread and anxiety. This avoidance behavior has led to a noticeable decrease in his professional engagement and satisfaction. Recently, Sai decided to seek help because his symptoms had begun to interfere with his daily life and work responsibilities to such an extent that he could no longer cope alone. He was most afraid of continuing down this path of isolation and self-blame, but at the same time, he hoped for a way to regain control over his thoughts and emotions. Sai's journey toward recovery is marked by both fear and hope; he fears the memories and triggers will continue to haunt him, but he also hopes that with support and understanding, he can find peace again. The interplay between his negative appraisals and intrusive memories has created a complex web of avoidance behaviors and emotional distress. Sai's experience of helplessness and self-blame are deeply intertwined with his memory of the event, making it difficult for him to distinguish between past trauma and present reality. This cycle has been tightening over time, but he is now ready to address these challenges head-on in therapy.
